claim: For stationary band-limited Gaussian noise of bandwidth Δν observed for a time τ there are N = 2Δν·τ independent samples, and its average power can be estimated with a fractional (normalized) uncertainty of (N/2)^(-1/2) = (Δν·τ)^(-1/2); the fractional error does not depend on the power level itself.

source.authors: Condon JJ, Ransom SM
source.title: Essential Radio Astronomy, Chapter 3: Radio Telescopes and Radiometers (online course text)
source.journal: National Radio Astronomy Observatory (book edition: Princeton University Press)

quote: an ideal radiometer can determine the average noise power with a fractional uncertainty as small as (N/2)^-1/2 = (Δν τ)^-1/2 ≪ 1
notes: Formula rendered from the page's MathML alt text '(N/2)^{-1/2}=(\Delta\nu\,\tau)^{-1/2}\ll 1'; N = 2Δν·τ is stated just before ('2 Δν τ independent samples'). Radio-astronomy setting (square-law detector on receiver noise), but the mathematics is that of band power of any band-limited Gaussian signal. For EEG band power, my arithmetic: B = 3 Hz, T = 1 s gives 0.58; T = 4 s gives 0.29. This is a floor for a stationary Gaussian rhythm; measured alpha power fluctuates more (t7-10, t7-13). The same chapter (3.6.3) notes that gain fluctuations with 1/f spectra set a practical floor, the analogue of slow EEG nonstationarity. Year 2016 is the print edition; the page is the NRAO online edition.

claim: Ideal total-power radiometer equation: the rms fluctuation of a noise-power estimate averaged over bandwidth Δν and time τ is σ_T ≈ T_s/sqrt(Δν·τ) (Eq. 3.154), obtained from N = 2Δν·τ independent samples each with rms error 2^(1/2)·T_s, giving σ_T = 2^(1/2)·T_s/N^(1/2) (Eq. 3.153).

source.authors: Condon JJ, Ransom SM

evidence_location: Section 3.6.2 'Radiometers', Eq. (3.153) and boxed Eq. (3.154); formal derivation referred to Appendix B.6
quote: In terms of bandwidth Δν and integration time τ, σ_T ≈ T_s/√(Δν τ) (3.154)
notes: Equation read from MathML alt text '\boxed{\sigma_{T}\approx\frac{T_{\mathrm{s}}}{\sqrt{\Delta\nu\,\tau}}}'. T_s is the mean noise power expressed as a temperature, so σ_T/T_s = 1/sqrt(Δν·τ) is the normalized random error. The text calls it 'the ideal radiometer equation for a total-power receiver'. Appendix B.6 (formal derivation) was not read.

claim: Bendat's approximate normalized random error of an averaged power spectral density estimate is ε_r = 1/sqrt(B_e·T_t), with B_e the effective (resolution) bandwidth and T_t the total data length; with B_e ≈ 1/T per segment and T_t = M·T this equals 1/sqrt(M) for M averaged segments.

notes: Abstract only (full text paywalled, not opened), so the band limits, electrodes and whether the range spans electrodes or subjects are unknown. The CV includes slow trends: alpha power fell towards the end of the recording, and lengthening the recording from 40 to 400 s raised the alpha CV by 36% (same abstract). Comparison (my arithmetic, assuming an 8 to 13 Hz band): a stationary Gaussian rhythm would give 1/sqrt(5 Hz x 4 s) = 0.22, so measured alpha power scatters about 3 times more than that floor, consistent with bursting (t7-12, t7-13) and long-range correlations (t7-14).

claim: Combining four motor-imagery tasks (left hand, right hand, foot, tongue) and mental arithmetic into subsets of 2 to 5 classes, information transfer rates ranged from 0.42 to 0.81 bits per trial in 3 subjects, and the best rates came from three-task subsets: adding a fourth or fifth task did not help.
units: mental tasks (upper limit for best information transfer)

source.authors: Obermaier B, Neuper C, Guger C, Pfurtscheller G
source.title: Information transfer rate in a five-classes brain-computer interface
source.journal: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering

quote: reveal that the upper limit of different mental tasks for a BCI system is three
notes: Abstract only; N = 3; band-power features with hidden Markov models. Same abstract: 'The achieved information transfer rates vary from 0.42 to 0.81 bits per trial' and 'different combinations of three tasks resulted in the best performance'. The limit is set by separability of the tasks, not by the electrode count; the paper does not say this in those words.

claim: Because many perceptual, memory and task-load processes also desynchronize alpha rhythms, more than two mental states are very hard to discriminate when only imagery-induced ERD is available; distinct classes need some tasks to produce ERS instead.

source.authors: Pfurtscheller G, Brunner C, Schlögl A, Lopes da Silva FH
source.title: Mu rhythm (de)synchronization and EEG single-trial classification of different motor imagery tasks

quote: it is very difficult to discriminate between more than two mental states when only imagery-induced ERD patterns are available.
notes: The preceding sentence of the Conclusion attributes this to alpha desynchronization by 'perceptual and memory processes and task complexity' (citing Klimesch 1999). The Conclusion also states that enhancement versus suppression across tasks is 'a prerequisite for an optimal distinctiveness'.

claim: Motor-imagery BCIs give low-dimensional control because they recognize only a limited number of mental tasks (typically left hand, right hand, foot); different movements of the same limb are hard to separate because their cortical representations are very close.

source.authors: Yong X, Menon C
source.title: EEG classification of different imaginary movements within the same limb

evidence_location: Introduction, first and second paragraphs; Abstract
quote: these systems have low dimensional control, i.e., they can only recognize a limited number of mental tasks as unique control commands.
notes: Open access, full text read. Introduction: 'these motor tasks activate regions that have very close representations on the motor cortex area of the brain'. Abstract: classifying same-limb imagery 'could increase the number of control dimensions'. A statement that dimensions are limited by distinguishable mental tasks, not by sensors, though not phrased as a sensor comparison.

claim: The small number of separable motor-imagery classes limits the number of output commands, which has motivated combined (compound) limb imagery to add classes.

source.authors: Yi W, Qiu S, Qi H, Zhang L, Wan B, Ming D
source.title: EEG feature comparison and classification of simple and compound limb motor imagery

quote: the limited numbers of classes contribute to the limited output commands
notes: Open access, full text read. The paper also reports that compound-imagery ERD bands 'overlap with that of the former one but more broad as well' (Results), i.e. compound classes reuse the same rhythms rather than adding independent ones. Class counts and accuracies of this paper were not re-checked here.

claim: Because mu and beta rhythm changes during movement and imagery differed in topography and in principal components, the authors suggest mu and beta might act as independent control signals, i.e. frequency may add channels beyond the few body parts.

source.authors: McFarland DJ, Miner LA, Vaughan TM, Wolpaw JR
source.title: Mu and beta rhythm topographies during motor imagery and actual movements

quote: suggest that mu and beta rhythms might provide independent control signals.
notes: Abstract only; a suggestion, not a demonstration of independent volitional control. A counterweight to 'only a few body parts': the count of separately modulable signals may exceed the count of body parts if mu and beta can be driven separately. According to the site's docs/research/section7-challenge.md (not re-checked here), McFarland et al. 2010 built its three dimensions from adaptive mixtures of 3-Hz-band amplitudes at C3, C4, Cz and CPz.
